Females of the Mountain bluebird (Sialia currucoides) typically lay 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 5 eggs per clutch] and produce 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = 2 clutches each year], an output that reflects a rapid pace of reproduction under favorable conditions. During the active breeding period, when ambient temperatures hover near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the energetic demands of incubation and provisioning are substantial. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is 3.2 grams [Ww0 = 3.2 grams], a value that aligns closely with those reported for other thrushes of similar body size. Eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after an incubation period of approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days], a duration typical for cavity-nesting passerines in open montane habitats. This relatively short developmental phase likely reduces predation risk during the vulnerable egg stage. The hatching success recorded at this incubation temperature is high, with over ninety percent of fertilized ova producing viable nestlings. These two fecundity parameters combine to yield a daily reproductive rate of approximately 0.027 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.027 eggs per day] when averaged across the breeding season.

Newly hatched chicks weigh approximately 3.14 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.14 grams], a modest neonatal mass that underscores the altricial condition of these nestlings. Under the sustained thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which matches the typical brood patch temperature of incubating and brooding females, the feather-growing nestlings progress through rapid somatic growth. The time since birth at fledging, defined as the age at which these young birds achieve sustained flight and depart the nest, is 20 days [tx = 20 days]. at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]This rapid transition from a helpless, pin-feathered chick to a flight-capable fledgling is characteristic of open-country species that face elevated nest predation pressure. The achievement of flight competence at this age allows the fledgling to escape ground-based predators and begin exploring its surroundings, though it remains dependent on parental provisioning for several additional weeks during the post-fledging refinement of foraging skills.

Sexual maturation in this species, marked by the onset of gonadal activity and the attainment of reproductive capability, occurs at 60 days since birth [tp = 60 days since birth] under the same thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively early puberty, completed before the onset of the first winter, suggests that individuals are anatomically prepared for breeding in their first spring. However, the time since birth at first brood, which corresponds to the age at which a female successfully lays her first clutch of the breeding season, is typically deferred until approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth] when measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This year-long delay between the attainment of sexual maturity and the first successful reproductive event likely reflects the constraints imposed by territory acquisition, pair bond formation, and the necessity of reaching adequate body condition before the substantial energetic investment of egg production and incubation can be undertaken.

The ultimate wet weight, or maximum recorded adult body mass, of a fully grown Mountain bluebird is 29.6 grams [Wwi = 29.6 grams]. This body size places the species among the smaller members of the thrush family, a group that includes both much larger congeners such as the Western bluebird and smaller, insectivorous specialists. Adult body condition fluctuates seasonally, with individuals reaching peak mass just prior to the onset of egg laying and declining notably during the demanding chick-rearing phase. Field records indicate that both sexes feed extensively on insects and berries during the breeding season, a diet that supports the high metabolic costs of sustained flight and territorial defense. The body mass of 29.6 grams [Wwi = 29.6 grams] is also consistent with the species' documented flight performance, which favors agility over speed in the pursuit of aerial insect prey above open meadows and forest clearings across its high-elevation range.

Maximum lifespan in the Mountain bluebird has been documented at 9 years [am = 9 years] under the thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterize its active metabolic period during spring and summer. This longevity is relatively modest among passerines, reflecting the species' occupation of climatically extreme montane and subalpine environments where winter survivorship can be low and the reproductive season is compressed into a few short months. Senescent individuals in the wild show declining reproductive output, reduced feather quality, and diminished territorial defense capabilities before natural mortality occurs. The interplay between a high daily reproductive rate of 0.027 eggs per day [Ri = 0.027 eggs per day], enabled by the production of 5 eggs per clutch over 2 clutches annually, and a comparatively finite lifespan underscores the rapid life-history strategy that characterizes this species. These demographic parameters position Sialia currucoides as a classic "fast-lived" bird in which early reproduction and high annual fecundity compensate for elevated adult mortality in unpredictable environments.
